overview: Both are genes added to a vector to help confirm successful gene transfer, but they signal success in very different ways.
genZNote: Selectable marker: kills off everyone who didn't get the gene. Reporter gene: lights up (sometimes literally) to show who did.

aspects.label: How Success Is Detected
aspects.valueA: Confers resistance (e.g. to an antibiotic) so only successfully transformed cells survive selection.
aspects.valueB: Produces an easily detectable, visible signal (colour, fluorescence, luminescence) in cells that took up the vector.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueB: Green fluorescent protein (GFP) gene, or the lacZ gene (blue-white screening).

aspects.label: Fate of Non-Transformed Cells
aspects.valueA: Non-transformed cells are killed or fail to grow during selection.
aspects.valueB: Non-transformed cells simply don't show the reporter signal, but aren't necessarily killed.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Blue-white screening using the lacZ reporter gene is a classic technique for visually distinguishing recombinant from non-recombinant bacterial colonies.
overlay.memoryTrick: Selectable marker = survival test. Reporter gene = visible signal.
overlay.commonMisconception: A selectable marker and a reporter gene are not mutually exclusive — a single vector often carries both, using one to select successful transformants and the other to confirm expression.
